title: Second stage, perineal care and trauma classification
blurb: Support pushing and protect the perineum in the second stage, classify perineal trauma correctly, and carry out a systematic assessment after birth.
question: After a spontaneous vaginal birth, Nadia's midwife sees a perineal tear that appears to involve the muscle and possibly the anal sphincter. How should the midwife assess the trauma, and how would a tear through more than half the external anal sphincter be classified?

teach.body: Formally: perineal trauma is any injury to the genital tract caused by tearing or episiotomy, classified by NICE NG235 from first degree (skin only) to fourth degree (anal sphincter complex and anal epithelium). In plain English: the midwife supports the woman to push in the way that suits her, uses simple measures to protect the perineum, avoids routine episiotomy, and after the birth carefully checks for tears, including any damage to the anal sphincter, so they can be repaired properly.

teach.body: Repair as soon as possible to reduce infection and blood loss, with tested, effective analgesia (infiltration, or top up an epidural). First degree: suture unless the skin edges are well opposed. Second degree: suture the muscle; if the skin is then opposed it need not be sutured; if it does, use a continuous subcuticular technique. Transfer (with the baby) to obstetric-led care if more expertise is needed. After forceps or ventouse, offer a single IV dose of co-amoxiclav within 6 hours of cord clamping.

The midwife explains what she needs to do, offers Entonox, ensures good lighting and positions Nadia comfortably once skin-to-skin is established and there is no heavy bleeding. With tested local analgesia in place she inspects the tear, its apex and bleeding, and performs a rectal examination because muscle damage is suspected. More than half the EAS thickness is torn: a 3b tear. She asks for obstetric review, documents with a diagram and transfers Nadia with her baby for repair.

teach.text: 3a vs 3b turns on the EXTERNAL sphincter (under or over 50%); 3c means the INTERNAL sphincter is torn; fourth degree adds the anal epithelium. And a previous third-degree tear is NOT a reason for routine episiotomy.

items: No epidural: spontaneous pushing; with epidural: delay pushing 1 h (multiparous) or up to 2 h (nulliparous).
Warm compress once the head distends the perineum, or massage if preferred; not in water births.
No routine episiotomy; if needed, mediolateral, usually right, 45 to 60 degrees, after tested analgesia.
Classification: 1st skin; 2nd muscle; 3a under 50% EAS; 3b over 50% EAS; 3c IAS; 4th plus epithelium.
Offer every woman systematic assessment including rectal examination.
Infibulated FGM: explain risks for VE, catheter and scalp electrode, and possible deinfibulation in labour.

summary: You can now support pushing in the second stage, use warm compresses or massage to protect the perineum, and explain when and how episiotomy is performed. You can also classify perineal trauma from first to fourth degree, carry out a systematic assessment with rectal examination, and know the first principles of repair.

A.q: When should the midwife offer to apply a warm compress to the perineum?
options: From confirmed full dilatation of the cervix
At the start of active pushing in the second stage
As soon as the baby's head has been born
Once the presenting part distends the perineum
A.why: NG235 1.9.13: once the presenting part distends the perineum in the second stage, offer a warm wet compress and continue until birth (not for births in water).

whyNot.0: Full dilatation is too early; the compress is applied when the perineum is distending.
whyNot.1: The trigger is perineal distension, not the onset of pushing.
whyNot.2: After the head is born is too late to protect the perineum.

A.q: How is a perineal tear involving more than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness classified?
options: 3b
3a
3c
Fourth degree
A.why: NG235 1.12.3: 3b is more than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness torn.

whyNot.1: 3a is less than 50% of the EAS thickness.
whyNot.2: 3c means the internal anal sphincter is torn.
whyNot.3: Fourth degree involves both sphincters and the anal epithelium.

A.q: An episiotomy is needed for a ventouse birth. There is no acute fetal compromise. What should happen first?
options: Lidocaine spray applied to the perineum
Entonox during the incision itself
Tested, effective analgesia is in place
No analgesia, as the perineum is stretched
A.why: NG235 1.9.23: provide tested, effective analgesia before an episiotomy, except in an emergency because of acute fetal compromise.

whyNot.0: Lidocaine spray is not offered in the second stage (1.9.15).
whyNot.1: Effective analgesia must be tested and in place before cutting.
whyNot.3: Stretching does not provide adequate analgesia.

B.q: Gina had a third-degree tear in her first birth. She is now in the second stage of her second labour, progressing well. What should the midwife do about episiotomy?
options: Perform a routine mediolateral episiotomy
No routine episiotomy
Perform an elective midline episiotomy
Perform an episiotomy as the head crowns
B.why: NG235 1.9.18: do not offer episiotomy routinely at vaginal birth after previous third- or fourth-degree trauma; her risk of repeat severe trauma is not increased compared with first-time mothers (1.9.17).

whyNot.0: Routine episiotomy is not recommended after previous severe trauma.
whyNot.2: A midline episiotomy is not the recommended technique and is not indicated.
whyNot.3: Episiotomy needs a clinical indication, not crowning alone.

B.q: Which women should be offered a systematic assessment including a rectal examination after a vaginal birth?
options: Women who had an instrumental birth
Women with a visible third-degree tear
Women with heavy bleeding after birth
All women, to exclude all genital trauma
B.why: NG235 1.12.5: offer all women systematic assessment, including a rectal examination, to exclude all genital tract trauma, including buttonhole tears.

whyNot.0: The offer applies to all women, not just after instrumental birth.
whyNot.1: Anal sphincter injury can be missed without a rectal examination even when not visible.
whyNot.2: Assessment is offered regardless of blood loss.

B.q: If an episiotomy is performed, which technique does NICE NG235 recommend?
options: Mediolateral, usually right, 45 to 60 degrees
Midline, straight down towards the anus
Mediolateral, left side, 15 to 30 degrees
J-shaped, curving laterally from the fourchette
B.why: NG235 1.9.21: mediolateral from the vaginal fourchette, usually directed to the right, at 45 to 60 degrees to the vertical at the time of the episiotomy.

whyNot.1: A midline cut towards the anus is not recommended.
whyNot.2: The recommended angle is 45 to 60 degrees.
whyNot.3: A J-shaped cut is not the NG235 technique.

C.q: Halima, 38 weeks, has infibulated FGM (type 3) and is in early labour. Which information should the midwife give her?
options: A planned caesarean birth is needed because of infibulation
A fetal scalp electrode is the preferred way to monitor
VE and catheter may be hard; deinfibulation may be needed
Spontaneous perineal tearing is less likely after FGM
C.why: NG235 1.9.20: inform women with infibulated FGM of difficulty with vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp electrodes, the risks of second-stage delay and spontaneous laceration, and possible deinfibulation in labour.

whyNot.0: Infibulation itself is not an indication for caesarean birth.
whyNot.1: Applying a fetal scalp electrode is one of the difficulties.
whyNot.3: There is a risk of spontaneous laceration.

C.q: Soon after birth, the midwife suspects Nadia's perineal muscles are torn. Skin-to-skin is established and there is no heavy bleeding. What is the correct approach?
options: Examine her fully before skin-to-skin is allowed to start
Explain, confirm analgesia, include a rectal examination
Defer all perineal assessment until the following day
Inspect the tear visually, without a rectal examination
C.why: NG235 1.12.7–1.12.8: explain, confirm tested effective analgesia, assess visually (structures, apex, bleeding) and perform a rectal examination if muscle damage is suspected, timed so it does not interfere with bonding.

whyNot.0: Assessment should not interfere with mother and baby bonding unless bleeding is urgent.
whyNot.2: Repair should be as soon as possible to reduce infection and blood loss.
whyNot.3: Suspected muscle damage needs a rectal examination to check the sphincters.

C.q: Kerry has had a forceps birth. Which antibiotic plan does NICE NG235 recommend?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days after the birth
IV co-amoxiclav before the forceps are applied
Antibiotics if she develops a fever later
IV co-amoxiclav within 6 hours of cord clamping
C.why: NG235 1.9.43: offer a single dose of IV co-amoxiclav (or local alternative if penicillin allergic) within 6 hours after cord clamping after forceps or ventouse birth.

whyNot.0: A course of oral antibiotics is not recommended.
whyNot.1: The dose is given after cord clamping, not before the instrument is applied.
whyNot.2: Prophylaxis is offered to all women after assisted birth, not just if fever develops.

reteach.title: Skin, muscle, sphincter, lining
reteach.question: Picture the perineum in layers from the outside in. How does each degree of tear add a layer?

blocks.body: First degree: the skin. Second: down into the perineal muscles. Third: into the anal sphincter complex, split by how much of the external sphincter is torn (3a under half, 3b over half) or whether the internal sphincter is torn (3c). Fourth: through both sphincters and into the anal lining (epithelium). A rectal examination is how sphincter damage is found.

blocks.text: 3a and 3b are about the EXTERNAL sphincter; 3c is the INTERNAL sphincter.

explain.body: Without an epidural, spontaneous pushing may shorten the second stage compared with directed pushing. With an epidural, pushing may be delayed 1 hour (multiparous) or up to 2 hours (nulliparous) unless she has an urge or the head is visible.

test.q: What advice about pushing should be given to a woman without an epidural in the second stage?
options: Spontaneous pushing may shorten the second stage
Directed breath-holding shortens it for everyone
Lying flat on her back helps her push effectively
She should start pushing from 8 cm dilatation
test.why: NG235 1.9.7: spontaneous pushing may shorten the second stage compared with directed pushing.

whyNot.1: NG235 does not recommend directed breath-holding for all women.
whyNot.2: Lying flat can reduce BP and placental blood flow.
whyNot.3: Active pushing is with full dilatation of the cervix.

explain.body: A second-degree tear involves the perineal muscles but not the anal sphincter. It is the commonest tear needing repair: suture the muscle, and the skin if it is not opposed afterwards.

test.q: Which description matches a second-degree perineal tear?
options: Injury to the perineal skin
Less than 50% of the EAS thickness torn
Perineal muscles, not the anal sphincter
The internal anal sphincter is torn
test.why: NG235 1.12.3: second degree is injury to the perineal muscles but not the anal sphincter.

whyNot.0: Skin only is a first-degree tear.
whyNot.1: Under 50% of the EAS is a 3a tear.
whyNot.3: A torn internal anal sphincter is a 3c tear.

explain.body: Suture the muscle to improve healing. If the skin is opposed after suturing the muscle, there is no need to suture it; if it does need suturing, use a continuous subcuticular technique.

test.q: After suturing the muscle in a second-degree tear, the skin edges are well opposed. What should the midwife do?
options: Close the skin with interrupted sutures
No need to suture the skin
Leave the muscle and close the skin
Close the skin with tissue glue
test.why: NG235 1.12.18: if the skin is opposed after suturing the muscle in second-degree trauma, there is no need to suture it.

whyNot.0: Skin suturing is not needed when edges are opposed; if needed, use continuous subcuticular.
whyNot.2: The muscle should be sutured to improve healing (1.12.17).
whyNot.3: Tissue glue is not the NG235 recommendation.

explain.body: In England and Wales, a regulated health professional who discovers that FGM has been carried out on a girl under 18 (told by her or seeing physical signs) must notify the police within one month (FGM Act 2003 s5B). For women 18 and over, carry out a safeguarding assessment.

test.q: Amina, 17, is in labour at a unit in England. Physical signs of FGM are seen. What legal duty applies to the midwife?
options: Report to social care within 48 hours
Record it; no report as she is pregnant
Report to the police within 12 months
Notify the police within one month
test.why: FGM Act 2003 s5B: a regulated professional who observes signs of FGM in a girl under 18 must notify the police before the end of one month from discovery.

whyNot.0: The mandatory duty is to the police, within one month.
whyNot.1: Pregnancy does not remove the duty for a girl under 18.
whyNot.2: The deadline is one month, not 12 months.
